It does. Teacher here who has been forced to work with CCSS for many years. Ask me anything.

As a teacher, what do you make of this unsupported claim? Or is there support? (I didn't find it)

The study, which was funded by the independent research liaison, Children First, found that average IQ’s declined a total of 10 points to an average of 98 when children were exposed to the curriculum for an entire academic year.
If this is true why would the states even adopt common core curriculum in the first place?

The problem with the CCSS is the fact that teachers are expected to teach standards at grade level. Well, in a perfect world, that is great, but most teachers are not living in that world. In my 6th grade class alone, I have students ranging from 2-10th grade reading levels. Well, there is no way a 2nd grade is going to understand development of theme, but perhaps I could teach them theme. You see, the standards are vertically aligned, which is great, but teachers are under so much pressure due to test scores, that they are scared to differentiate. What I mean is, my students are going to be tested 6th grade PAARC, and it does not matter if they showed growth because the test does not measure growth! It just measures whether or not the students meet he standard.

Now the other problem is, even if my students are reading at a 6th grade level, the test is completely unfair. It is not testing reading levels - it is testing whether or not they met the standard, but some of the standards are tested ridiculously.

The questions are unfair to students and super tricky. My students are supposed to be able to write an entire essay independently (not a big deal) on development techniques an author uses! You think that is easy to teach a 6th grader? Think again.

So, what happens is, teachers are all over the place in how to teach. There is really no great way to teach the CCSS. I seriously push myself and my students so hard. Now, my test scores were excellent last year, so I'm doing something right, but...I honestly am teaching my students how to 'beat' the questions. That is insane. That is not what a classroom is supposed to be about.

There is way more. I'm going to start an AMA. I'll link it here.
How much does the CCSS control how you teach? I understand you have to teach to the test but does it also control lesson plans?
It controls every single aspect of my teaching unfortunately.

Is there a method to the madness, or is it as stupid as it appears at first glance? I read that it was meant to encourage critical thinking, and although the initial phases are arbitrary when used in simple mathematics, the rules become very useful later on in calculus.

I personally suck at math but I've always excelled at language, and critical thinking is one of my strongest personality traits. I sometimes wonder if I had learned through this system, whether math would have gone better for me. I did try in class, straight A's everywhere else, advanced classes and gifted programs everywhere but math, and a high IQ. But the logic I applied to mathematical problems was always the wrong way to do it. My brain just doesn't work that way I guess, so I wonder if maybe this would have helped? I feel pretty mathematically crippled now as an adult, I never did take to the 'right' way to solve problems.

Are there any kids that sucked before and do better with this system?

There is a method, and I definitely get what you're saying.

The problem is (unfortunately for you) most students do not learn that way. You probably were not supported for your different learning style, which isn't fair to you. I think teachers do a better job today of differentiating for unique learning styles.

At the same time, the CCSS (specifically in math), does not allow for that. It is teaching there is 'one right way to teach this' but in a different way. This is ridiculous. Teachers should be able to let their students (at least to an extent) utilize their learning styles to learn! Sounds crazy, doesn't it? haha.

So, they aren't allowing students to memorize as much anymore. This can be a problem though. For example, in 6th grade I memorized all of the figurative language. Now, I probably didn't see the value of that in 6th grade, but as my brain developed, I could apply what I learned later on.

The problem is the CCSS is not taking in account the way our brains develop. For example, abstract concepts like theme are really really difficult for even the smartest 6th graders to grasp. But they do not just want students to identify theme - no students have to write a 5 paragraph essay on how theme is developed. The thing is, it can literally take one student an entire year just the grasp the idea of theme.

Now, don't get me wrong. I am not against the CCSS themselves. I'm against how they are just another money making system. I support critical thinking, but my job shouldn't be on the line and there should be a variety of factors evaluated. The CCSS does not measure poverty and how it impacts learning!! So these standards might be great for wealthier, upper class areas, but they aren't for my students.

Sorry that was a lot of rambling. I'm going to do an AMA.

You should totally do an AMA! I think most adults are completely baffled by the 'new math'. Your insights are really helpful and interesting.

You're right - each brain is different and forcing them all into a particular way of thinking is disadvantageous for many. Especially when it prevents you, as a teacher, from teaching in a more effective manner per as per an individual student's needs. That's sort of BS actually. I didn't realize that you weren't even allowed to tailor things or work with different learning styles. I thought the job of a teacher was to teach effectively, which clearly, this is not...

I completely agree. And, it's not that we can't tailor things to an extent, but I'm expected to get a student with a 3rd grade reading level to understand a 6th grade standard. I should be working on helping improve their reading comprehension!
